headlines.summary: Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date.
headlines.article_text: Tesla Roadster reveal: What to know about the delayed EV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster from a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday. CEO Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date. Tesla said the new Roadster, equipped with SpaceX thrusters, can accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second. In this article TSLA SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 8:08 08:08 Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster, showing off its flying-car ambitions Squawk Box Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering. "You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026, in this still image taken from a handout video. Tesla | Via Reuters The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company. At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground. The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience. Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster. It was unclear whether the vehicle would be street-legal, with Musk saying on stage that "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car." The Roadster unveiling has added to speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX. For years, Musk's companies have worked with and paid each other, even sharing some personnel. The collaboration has increased in 2026, with speculation about a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger swirling since the aerospace and defense company went public in June. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC ahead of the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier." Barclays analyst Dan Levy predicted in a note out this week that such a merger could happen before the end of 2026. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026 Source: Tesla Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly." The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics. One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver. Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealing a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event in Waco, Texas, US, on October 15, 2026 Source: Tesla Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." After the event, O'Connor said what he saw was "off the charts." Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: TSLA, SPCX, AA, CRWV Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket: Tesla — Shares climbed nearly 5% after the EV maker unveiled its long-awaited second-generation Roadster . The vehicle uses SpaceX-developed rocket-style thrusters and demonstrated aerial maneuvers at the event Thursday. Tesla describes it as the world's first flying car and expects production to begin in 2028. SpaceX — The rocket company also got a boost from the Tesla Roadster unveil, rising more than 1%. A price target increase from Evercore ISI and rival Blue Origin laying out plans to ramp New Glenn launches to multiple flights per week by the end of the decade lifted the stock as well. Alcoa — The aluminum producer rose more than 2% on better-than-expected earnings for the third quarter, helped by a rebound in its alumina business . CoreWeave — Shares of the compute provider fell 4% premarket as Thursday's rebound appeared to be short-lived. The stock has come under pressure this week as investors brace for higher interest rates that might impact the highly indebted company. Netflix — Shares fell nearly 1.5% premarket after the streaming giant announced a leadership shake-up. Chief content officer Bela Bajaria is leaving the company and will be replaced by former Disney executive Peter Rice. The change comes only a day after Netflix said it would cut roughly 6% of its workforce , or about 1,000 jobs. Travelers — The insurance giant fell 4% even after the company reported third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations. Travelers posted core third-quarter earnings of $9.18 per share on revenue of $12.48 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG expected a profit of $7.42 per share on revenue of $11.38 billion. — CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed reporting
